source_batch.unit_label: Module D unit 4 (courseware unit 29): identification of compliance issues and compliance risks

facts.statement: Compliance and compliance issues (courseware): compliance is the act of following laws, rules, regulations and codes of conduct, including the voluntary ones; most arise from external requirements but adherence to the organisation's own rules, policies and procedures, and acting in accordance with ethical practices, is equally important. A compliance issue is a single event during which any Accountable Employee is in violation of one or more processes or procedures required under the Rules. Compliance challenges for banks and financial institutions the courseware lists: geopolitical trends towards nationalism and protectionism (uncertainty in data protection, KYC and beneficial ownership regulation); divergence in regulation across jurisdictions ("merge the diverge") in cybersecurity, data privacy, loan servicing and customer and industry related banking, supervisory expectations that deviate from global standards, new technology applications and non-financial and statutory regulators; protection and governance of data (including data held by third parties); operational resilience through continuity planning, operational risk and concentration risk analysis, including cyber-crime, environmental and socio-political threats; credit cycle risks (risk layering and leveraged lending, expanded delivery channels, new products and technology, disclosures, lending to non-depository institutions, climate and health effects on production); easing of regulatory capital and liquidity requirements in some countries, which does not mean weaker risk management; agility of compliance operations as technology moves; the fine line between innovation and financial crime; building customer trust through personalised service, data privacy and fair value; and ethics in business (privacy, sales processes, fair treatment, incentive plans, market conduct, third-party oversight).

Compliance risk and how it is identified (courseware): the Basel Committee on compliance function defines compliance risk as the risk of legal or regulatory sanctions, material financial loss, or loss to reputation a bank may suffer as a result of its failure to comply with laws, regulations, rules, related self-regulatory organisation standards and codes of conduct applicable to its banking activities. Common compliance risks include corruption, employee behaviour, workplace health and safety, environmental impact, data management, quality, process and social responsibility. The level of compliance risk in each business line, product and process is identified on regulatory focus, customer service aspect, control aspects, nature of activity (whether inherently high risk), the bank's exposure (materiality), major breaches reported in the past (history) and penalty implications. The bank has a new product approval process so compliance risk mitigants are in place before launch; the compliance officer is a member of the new product approval committee. The CCO participates in the quarterly informal discussions held with RBI, keeps contact with the SSM team and RBI, and the compliance staff have access to information to conduct compliance reviews and investigations. Staff accountability is examined for all compliance failures and the bank designs a system to give due weightage to the record of compliance in performance appraisal. As part of corporate governance the compliance function is independent and sufficiently resourced, has clearly defined responsibilities, is subject to periodic independent review by internal audit, and is a core risk management activity that is not outsourced.
facts.locator: S01 printed pp. 617-618; policy and review rules confirmed by RBI_CCO_2020 paragraph 2.1

facts.statement: Compliance risk management function and due diligence (courseware): historically compliance was reactive and had limited modelling; the present approach is risk based with due diligence, meaning the organisation can show it was diligent in meeting obligations through a management system that is effective and not merely on paper or legalistic, emphasises results and not only process, and has working procedures that tell staff what to do. Essential ingredients of due diligence: real commitment to compliance; a pro-active culture; consistent and effective enforcement (discipline, investigation, corrective and preventive action); full and effective reporting and action; adequate resources; monitoring, audit and inspection to be satisfied the system works; identifying and assessing requirements as they affect the business; outsourcing or contractual obligations with required standards monitored; identifying and managing risk exposure; and measuring the level of compliance. The complete function includes, on a pro-active basis, identifying, documenting and assessing compliance risks including from new products, customer relationships and business changes; advising committees on integrity and reputational issues (such as checks on borrowing clients and project sponsors); leading and coordinating investigations into alleged unsatisfactory conduct or misconduct of employees under the guidance of the CMD, with the head of internal audit and compliance; dealing with conflicts of interest, money laundering, terrorist financing and complaints on bank-financed operations; developing measures of compliance risk; assessing the bank's regulatory framework and proposing amendments; reviewing the Code of Conduct; running a risk based annual compliance programme overseen by the head of compliance; reporting regularly to the Audit Committee and CMD on assessment, testing, breaches and corrective action; and cooperating closely with internal audit.

Operational risk, inherent and residual risk (courseware): operational risk is the risk of loss resulting from inadequate or failed internal processes, people and systems or from external events; the definition includes legal risk but excludes strategic and reputational risk. External causes range from floods and earthquakes to power failures and terrorist attacks; internal causes include failures of IT, risk management or HR systems, outsourced service providers, mismanaged or poorly trained employees, negligence, wilful misconduct, conflict of interest and fraud. Mistrust, failure to communicate, low morale, cynicism and increased staff turnover indicate a potential increase in operational risk. Inherent risk is the risk a system poses out of the box, before any processes, technologies or people are put in place (courseware: inherent risk = threats x vulnerability); residual risk is the probability of loss that remains after controls have been implemented (courseware: residual risk = inherent risk x control risk). The courseware's example is crossing a street: looking left and right reduces the very high inherent risk but cannot remove the residual risk.

Main inherent risks (courseware): credit risk is the risk of loss when customers' financial condition deteriorates and principal and interest cannot be recovered; the bank gives it the highest priority and relies on credit rating and self-assessment systems. Market risk is the possibility of loss from movements in interest rates, foreign exchange rates, stock prices and other market indicators, and includes credit risk inherent in market transactions (counterparties failing to meet obligations); risk volumes (limits on maximum volume of risk and loss) are decided by the Board and the Executive Committee, operations stay within assigned limits, results of operations and profit or loss are reported daily to the directors in charge and monthly to the Executive Committee. Liquidity risk is the risk of running short of funds because of falling creditworthiness or an extreme gap between maturities of inflows and outflows, forcing borrowing at high rates; the bank examines the structure of fund sources and uses, sets guidelines on the funds gap (the amount that must be raised), reports to the Risk management department, which is in overall charge of cash flow management, and has contingency plans. Operations risk arises in handling customer transactions (errors, unethical conduct, disparities in cash balances, complaints); the operations department is in overall charge, improving procedures and supervising branch operations, and the Inspection department does internal checking including overseas offices. Systems risk arises from malfunctions and unethical conduct in computer systems and is managed as part of a bank-wide management system, with multiple telecommunications lines, backup computer centres and a systems office within the planning department for monitoring.

Compliance risk assessment (courseware): assessment is the process of assessing the level of compliance with regulatory directives affecting the bank and the major compliance risks it faces; areas to look at include observations in regulatory examination reports, compliance testing, implementation of regulatory guidelines, regulatory reporting and compliance culture, and for overseas establishments regulatory examination reports, enforcement action, closure of audit reports, implementation of guidelines, regulatory reporting, AML-CFT compliance and training. The courseware's scale of 1 to 10: a score of 7.1 to 10 means needs significant improvement; 5.1 to 7 needs improvement; 3.1 to 5 meets requirement; 1 to 3 is well controlled. The plan to mitigate the risks: assess compliance risk activity-wise at least once a year and develop a risk-oriented activity plan submitted to the ACB for approval and made available to internal audit; report promptly to the Board, ACB or MD and CEO on major changes or observations; periodically report failures and breaches to the Board or ACB and circulate to functional heads; examine sustenance of compliance as part of testing and annual assessment; and ensure compliance with supervisory observations of RBI and other directions in letter and spirit in a time bound and sustainable manner. The quality assurance and improvement programme covers all aspects of the compliance function and is independently externally reviewed at least once in three years. Compliance is a shared responsibility of the business units and the compliance function; adherence to statutory provisions and regulations is the responsibility of every staff member and it is the compliance function's work to ensure it.
facts.locator: S01 printed pp. 623-624; annual assessment, plan, reporting and three-year review confirmed by RBI_CCO_2020 paragraphs 2.1 and 2.9

facts.statement: Independent testing and an effective audit programme (courseware): compliance units evaluate compliance risk in each business line periodically and report to the Board or management committee. Key components of an effective audit programme: an appropriate policy for the institution's risk profile; coverage of all applicable regulations and guidance; effective scoping and planning; adequate transaction testing; no gaps in the programme; well-organised work papers and clear paper trails; communication of exceptions; identification of violations and explanation of risks; recommending and tracking corrective action; communicating results to the Board, Audit Committee and senior management; documenting resolution of observations not carried into the audit report. An efficient compliance policy also documents the understanding of the AML risk profile, identifies high risk services, products and clients, considers new regulations since the prior audit, recent audit and examination results and past recommendations, and changes since the prior audit (risk profile, the compliance function, new guidelines, IT enhancements, monitoring parameters, key staff, new products). Areas tested include adequacy of policies, high risk customer identification, customer due diligence and enhanced due diligence, customer identification programme, internal controls and reporting, suspicious activity monitoring, record keeping, bank risk assessment, cash transaction reports and ATM and cash aggregation, with all actionable issues tracked, corrective action completed and closure validated. Testing can be by an independent audit function in the institution, head office audit, or an outside audit firm; staff doing the testing should have the technical expertise and specialised training in compliance regulations.

Reporting framework for compliance certificates (courseware): (a) branches and other operating units certify compliance with all regulatory and internal guidelines, including a separate certificate for KYC and AML compliance, to the regional or zonal office quarterly, as on the last working day of the quarter, within 5 days of closure of the quarter; (b) the regional or zonal office sends a consolidated certificate to the Compliance department at central office quarterly within 10 days of closure, and makes a copy available to the Risk officer for random test checking; (c) the head of each functional department at head office or corporate office certifies compliance to the Compliance department quarterly within 10 days of closure, on the basis of the list of compliance issues and RBI and MOF circulars sent during the quarter; (d) overseas branches certify compliance with local laws and the guidelines applicable in their countries to the Compliance department at the corporate office monthly within 5 days of completion of the month, through the Chief Executive of the centre with a copy to the International Department at head office. Breaches are reported in the structured format to the Compliance department at central office with a copy to the FGMO and the functional department, from branch, RO or ZO officials' visits, audit reports or surveys; functional departments and overseas branches report similarly; the audit department gives a copy of its report on breaches to the Compliance department and the controlling regional office. For random test checking the sample considers regulatory focus, whether the activity is inherently high risk, the bank's exposure, past major breaches, the same branches not repeated each time, and KYC and AML compliance at branch level.

Inspection and audit (courseware): inspection is typically a visit to the site required as part of a compliance obligation; audit is the process of checking that compliance obligations have been met, including that the required inspections were done. Inspections deal with things that can cause immediate accidents or other problems, while audits cover their root causes; both are vital. The courseware lists ten types of audit: risk based internal audit, concurrent audit, statutory audit and tax audit, credit audit, forensic audit, RBI inspections, system audit, stock audit, foreign exchange audit and snap audit. Banks conduct risk based internal audit through their Inspection and Audit departments; auditors capture breaches and report them to the Chief Compliance Officer at head office with a copy to the risk management department at the administrative or controlling office, which uses the reporting in random sample testing of compliances. The Audit Committee role includes: directing and overseeing the operations of the total audit function and the quality of internal audit and inspection; following up on observations of the statutory audit and RBI inspection (ISE); strengthening housekeeping; fixing accountability of inspecting or auditing officials for failure to detect serious irregularities; periodically reviewing accounting policies and internal control systems to ensure greater transparency; sensitising the Board about risk prone areas; reviewing risk management measures; and ensuring implementation of statutory compliances, including discussions with auditors on internal control systems and the half-yearly and annual statements, with authority to investigate and full access to information and external professional advice.

Loan review mechanism (courseware): a loan review assesses the overall quality of the loan portfolio, specifically individual loans (including repayment risk), compliance with lending procedures and policies, lapses in documentation, credit risk management priority findings and recommended practices; where banks risk-rate loans it also evaluates risk grades and their accuracy. A loan review is not a portfolio review (it does not assess geographic, borrower or other concentrations), not a portfolio trend analysis (it assesses loan quality at a point in time, though trends may be seen from the sample) and not an assessment of the loan loss reserve. Model checklist: credit initiation (eligibility, underwriting, financial statements analysis, primary and secondary repayment sources, management, appraisal); loan structuring (repayment terms against ability to repay, industry best practice, guarantees, environmental indemnification); loan approval procedures; credit and collateral file documentation; normal loan monitoring; problem loan management (reporting to senior management and downgrading of delinquent loans); loan workout management; and a report of findings, conclusions and recommendations to the competent authority.

Credit audit (courseware): RBI guidelines on credit risk management say credit risk is the most important aspect of bank fund management; credit audit is a mid-course correction after sanction, examining compliance with sanction and post-sanction processes. Objectives: improve the quality of the credit portfolio; review the sanction process and compliance status of large loans; give feedback on regulatory compliance; independently review credit risk assessment; pick up early warning signals and suggest remedial measures; recommend corrective action to improve credit quality, credit administration and credit skills of staff. The credit audit or loan review mechanism may sit in a specific department or in the Inspection and Audit department; its functions are to process credit audit reports, analyse findings and advise departments, follow up with controlling authorities, apprise top management, process responses and arrange closure, and maintain a database of advances audited. Scope: portfolio review (quality of credit and investment portfolio, reducing concentrations to levels in the loan policy and RBI prudential norms) and loan review (all fresh proposals and renewals within 3 to 6 months from sanction; all existing accounts with limits at or above a cut-off depending on the size of activity; a random 5 to 10 per cent of the rest; accounts of sister, group and associate concerns even if the limit is below the cut-off); action points include checking compliance with policies and regulations, documentation, credit risk assessment, conduct of account, serious irregularities and early warning signals. Frequency: 3 months for high risk accounts, 6 months for average risk and 1 year for low risk. Procedure: credit audit is on site at the branch that appraised the advance and where the main operative limits are available; the report covers conduct of accounts of all allocated limits by calling for details from the corresponding branches; credit auditors need not visit borrowers' premises.

What good compliance delivers (courseware): regulators and professionals struggle to explain how integrated governance, risk and compliance (GRC) translates into bottom-line benefits; compliance should not be justified only by regulatory and legal requirements and fear of fines and reputational harm but also by its operational advantages, supported by indicators of programme effectiveness: an aligned operating strategy, effective oversight mechanisms, integrated risk and control activities, resource and personnel optimisation, streamlined business processes, and quality data and information. Key benefits: higher quality information (integrated GRC information lets management decide more rapidly), process optimisation (non-value-adding activities eliminated), better capital allocation (redundancy and inefficiency identified), improved effectiveness (activities directed to the right people and departments), protected reputation and reduced costs (contributing to return on investment).

payload.title: Operational risk, inherent risk and residual risk
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Operational risk:** loss from **inadequate or failed internal processes, people and systems**, or from **external events**. It **includes legal risk** and **excludes strategic and reputational risk**.

- **External causes:** floods, earthquakes, power failure, terrorism.
- **Internal causes:** failure of **IT, risk management or HR systems**, **outsourced providers**, poorly trained staff, **negligence**, **misconduct**, **conflict of interest**, **fraud**.
- **Warning signs of rising operational risk:** **mistrust**, **failure to communicate**, **low morale**, **cynicism**, **higher staff turnover**.

**Inherent vs residual (courseware):**

| Term | Meaning | Courseware formula |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Inherent risk** | Risk a system poses **out of the box**, **before controls** | **Threats x vulnerability** |
| **Residual risk** | Risk **left after controls** | **Inherent risk x control risk** |

Crossing a street: **looking both ways** lowers the high inherent risk, but a small **residual risk** remains.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Controls never reduce risk to zero, so residual risk always remains.

payload.title: Assessing compliance risk and planning to mitigate it
payload.core_explanation_md:

| Score | Level |
| --- | --- |
| **1 to 3** | **Well controlled** |
| **3.1 to 5** | **Meets requirement** |
| **5.1 to 7** | **Needs improvement** |
| **7.1 to 10** | **Needs significant improvement** |

payload.title: Independent testing and an effective audit programme

items.core_explanation_md:
**Compliance** means following **laws, rules, regulations and codes of conduct**, including voluntary ones, plus the bank's **own policies** and **ethical practice**.

| **Data** | **Protect and govern** data, including with **third parties** |
| **Operational resilience** | **Continuity planning**, **operational risk**, **concentration risk**, cyber and environmental threats |
| **Credit cycles** | **Risk layering**, leveraged lending, new channels, climate and health effects |
| **Capital and liquidity easing** (in some countries) | Does **not** mean weaker risk management |
| **Agility** | Keeping up with technology and regulatory change |
| **Innovation vs financial crime** | Technology helps both |
| **Customer trust** | Personalised service, privacy, **fair value** |
| **Ethics** | Privacy, sales processes, fair treatment, **incentive plans**, market conduct, third-party oversight |

items.title: Compliance risk management and due diligence
items.core_explanation_md:
Compliance used to be **reactive** (fixing problems after they appeared). Today it is **risk based**, with **due diligence**: the bank can **show it was diligent** because its system is **effective, not just on paper**, focuses on **results as well as process**, and has **working procedures**.

**Essential ingredients of due diligence:** **real commitment**; a **pro-active culture**; **consistent enforcement** (discipline, investigation, corrective and preventive action); **full reporting and action**; **adequate resources**; **monitoring, audit and inspection**; **identifying requirements** that affect the business; monitoring **outsourcing obligations**; **managing risk exposure**; **measuring compliance**.

**The complete function (courseware):** identify and assess risks from **new products and relationships**; advise committees on **integrity and reputation** (checks on borrowing clients and project sponsors); **investigate misconduct** under the CMD's guidance with the head of audit and compliance; handle **conflicts of interest, money laundering, terror financing** and **complaints on bank-financed operations**; **measure compliance risk**; **review the regulatory framework and the Code of Conduct**; run a **risk based annual programme**; **report to the Audit Committee and CMD**; cooperate with **internal audit**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A paper-only system fails due diligence even if every rule is documented.

self_check.prompt_text: What makes a compliance system pass due diligence according to the courseware?
self_check.expected_takeaway: It is effective in practice, not merely on paper, and focuses on results as well as process.

items.title: Operational risk, inherent risk and residual risk
items.core_explanation_md:
**Operational risk:** loss from **inadequate or failed internal processes, people and systems**, or from **external events**. It **includes legal risk** and **excludes strategic and reputational risk**.

- **External causes:** floods, earthquakes, power failure, terrorism.
- **Internal causes:** failure of **IT, risk management or HR systems**, **outsourced providers**, poorly trained staff, **negligence**, **misconduct**, **conflict of interest**, **fraud**.
- **Warning signs of rising operational risk:** **mistrust**, **failure to communicate**, **low morale**, **cynicism**, **higher staff turnover**.

**Inherent vs residual (courseware):**

| Term | Meaning | Courseware formula |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Inherent risk** | Risk a system poses **out of the box**, **before controls** | **Threats x vulnerability** |
| **Residual risk** | Risk **left after controls** | **Inherent risk x control risk** |

Crossing a street: **looking both ways** lowers the high inherent risk, but a small **residual risk** remains.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Controls never reduce risk to zero, so residual risk always remains.

self_check.prompt_text: Does the operational risk definition include strategic and reputational risk?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No; it includes legal risk but excludes strategic and reputational risk.

items.title: Assessing compliance risk and planning to mitigate it
items.core_explanation_md:
**Compliance risk assessment** gauges how well the bank complies with **regulatory directives** and which **major compliance risks** it faces. Evidence includes **regulatory examination observations**, **compliance testing**, **implementation of guidelines**, **regulatory reporting** and **compliance culture**; for **overseas establishments** also **enforcement action**, **closure of audit reports**, **AML-CFT compliance** and **training**.

**Courseware scale (illustrative):**

| Score | Level |
| --- | --- |
| **1 to 3** | **Well controlled** |
| **3.1 to 5** | **Meets requirement** |
| **5.1 to 7** | **Needs improvement** |
| **7.1 to 10** | **Needs significant improvement** |

**Mitigation plan:** assess **activity-wise at least yearly** and send a **risk-oriented activity plan to the ACB**, copied to **internal audit**; **report major changes promptly**; **report failures and breaches periodically**; check **sustenance**; meet **RBI's supervisory observations in letter and spirit, on time**.

**Shared responsibility:** **business units and the compliance function** share it, **every employee** must comply, and the **compliance function ensures** it.

items.title: Independent testing and an effective audit programme
items.core_explanation_md:
Compliance units **test compliance risk in each business line** periodically and put the results before the **Board or management committee**.

**An effective audit programme** has: a policy suited to the **risk profile**; coverage of **all applicable regulations**; good **scoping and planning**; **adequate transaction testing**; **no gaps**; organised **work papers and paper trails**; clear **exception reporting**; **identified violations and explained risks**; **recommended and tracked corrective action**; results reported to the **Board, Audit Committee and senior management**; documented resolution of observations not in the audit report.

**Before each cycle** consider: the **AML risk profile**, **high risk products and customers**, **new regulations**, **recent audit and examination results**, **past recommendations**, and **changes** in risk profile, the compliance function, IT, monitoring parameters, key staff and products.

**Areas tested (examples):** **policies**, **customer due diligence and enhanced due diligence**, **customer identification programme**, **internal controls and reporting**, **suspicious activity monitoring**, **record keeping**, **cash transaction reports**; **issues tracked to closure and closure validated**.

**Who tests:** an **independent audit function**, **head office audit** or an **outside audit firm**, with **technical expertise and training**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Validating closure matters because an issue marked closed on paper may still be open in practice.

self_check.prompt_text: Who may carry out the testing of compliance?
self_check.expected_takeaway: An independent audit function in the institution, head office audit or an outside audit firm, with the right expertise.

items.title: Inspection versus audit, and the types of audit
items.core_explanation_md:
Held at needs_review (courseware).

- **Inspection:** a **site visit** required as part of a compliance obligation. It deals with things that can cause **immediate accidents or problems**.
- **Audit:** checks that **compliance obligations have been met**, including that inspections were done. It covers the **root causes**.

Both are vital.

**Ten types of audit the courseware lists:** **risk based internal audit**, **concurrent audit**, **statutory and tax audit**, **credit audit**, **forensic audit**, **RBI inspections**, **system audit**, **stock audit**, **foreign exchange audit**, **snap audit**.

**Reporting:** internal auditors capture **breaches** and report them to the **CCO at head office** with a copy to **risk management** at the administrative or controlling office, which uses them in its **random testing of compliance**.

**The Audit Committee's audit role (courseware):** oversee the **whole audit function**, follow up **statutory audit and RBI inspection** findings, **strengthen housekeeping**, fix **accountability of auditors who miss serious irregularities**, review **accounting policies and internal controls**, **sensitise the Board to risk-prone areas**, review **risk management measures** and **ensure statutory compliances**; it can **investigate** and take **external advice**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Audit looks for why a problem arose; inspection looks at what is wrong now.

self_check.prompt_text: Which looks at root causes, inspection or audit?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Audit.

items.title: The loan review mechanism
items.core_explanation_md:
Held at needs_review (courseware).

A **loan review** assesses the **quality of the loan portfolio**: **individual loans** and **repayment risk**, **compliance with lending policies**, **documentation lapses**, **priority findings** and **recommended practices**. Where loans are risk-rated, it tests the **risk grades and their accuracy**.

| A loan review **is** | A loan review is **not** |
| --- | --- |
| Assessment of **individual loans** at a **point in time** | A **portfolio review** (no view of **concentrations**) |
| Quality, compliance and documentation findings | A **trend analysis** |
| Report to the **competent authority** | An assessment of the **loan loss reserve** |

**Checklist:** **credit initiation** (eligibility, underwriting, repayment sources, management, appraisal); **loan structuring**; **approval procedures**; **credit and collateral file documentation**; **normal monitoring**; **problem loan management** (reporting and downgrading); **loan workout**.
